extracted.intended_audience: educated readers, political philosophers, legislators, and anyone interested in critique of civil society and government
extracted.subtask_description: Identify and judge political institutions and forms of government by reference to natural standards (truth, virtue, liberty) and by their practical effects (protection from evils, production of violence, oppression).

rubrics_metrics.name: Conformity to truth and natural relations
rubrics_metrics.description: All happiness is connected with the practice of virtue, which necessarily depends upon the knowledge of truth; that is, upon the knowledge of those unalterable relations which Providence has ordained that every thing should bear to every other.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge institutions by whether they conform to these unalterable relations (truth). The essay insists that truth is the foundation of virtue and the only measure of happiness; institutions ought therefore to be evaluated by their alignment with that truth rather than by artifices or conveniences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conformity to nature (avoid forcing nature with artificial regulations)
rubrics_metrics.description: To these we should conform in good earnest; and not think to force nature, and the whole order of her system, by a compliance with our pride and folly, to conform to our artificial regulations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer explanations and institutions that 'conform to nature.' Policies or laws that force unnatural social structures or contradict human nature are to be viewed with suspicion; the author treats conformity to natural order as a key evaluative standard.

rubrics_metrics.name: Promotion of reason and rejection of superstition
rubrics_metrics.description: We begin to think and to act from reason and from nature alone. The miseries derived to mankind from superstition under the name of religion, and of ecclesiastical tyranny under the name of church government, have been clearly and usefully exposed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess religious and civil institutions by their reliance on reason and natural principles rather than on superstition or ecclesiastical tyranny. Institutions that propagate superstition or derive authority from 'artificial revelations' lose moral legitimacy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Government's effectiveness: protector from natural evils and increaser of blessings
rubrics_metrics.description: It is therefore of the deepest concernment to us to be set right in this point; and to be well satisfied whether civil government be such a protector from natural evils, and such a nurse and increaser of blessings, as those of warm imaginations promise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate governments by concrete effects: Do they alleviate natural evils and increase human blessings? This is a practical metric—governments are defensible only insofar as they serve these functions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Two-fold view of a state: external and internal relations
rubrics_metrics.description: In looking over any state to form a judgment on it, it presents itself in two lights; the external, and the internal. The first, that relation which it bears in point of friendship or enmity to other states. The second, that relation which its component parts, the governing and the governed, bear to each other.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Any evaluation of a state should explicitly consider (a) external relations (friendship/enmity, war/peace), and (b) internal relations (governing vs governed). Both perspectives are necessary; the text emphasizes that history is dominated by the external (war) but that internal relations determine justice and welfare.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contribution to large-scale violence and slaughter
rubrics_metrics.description: I now come to show that political society is justly chargeable with much the greatest part of this destruction of the species... Society and politics... have given us also the means of satisfying [destructive ends]... from the first rude essays of clubs and stones, to the present perfection of gunnery... which make a principal part of what politicians have taught us to believe is our principal glory.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measure political societies by their role in enabling or amplifying mass violence. The author quantifies historical slaughter to argue that political organization both motivates and materially enables enormous carnage; systems that do so are condemned.

rubrics_metrics.name: Degree of enforced subordination and its tendency to tyranny
rubrics_metrics.description: As subordination, or, in other words, the reciprocation of tyranny and slavery, is requisite to support these societies; the interest, the ambition, the malice, or the revenge, nay, even the whim and caprice of one ruling man among them, is enough to arm all the rest, without any private views of their own, to the worst and blackest purposes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate how much a polity depends on enforced subordination. The more a society requires strict hierarchical obedience, the more it creates conditions for tyranny and abuse—this is an intrinsic structural critique to be applied when judging institutions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Political distinctions and names as sources of hatred and dissension
rubrics_metrics.description: The artificial division of mankind into separate societies is a perpetual source in itself of hatred and dissension... The names which distinguish them are enough to blow up hatred and rage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess how much political or national labels foster hatred and dehumanization. Policies or rhetoric that emphasize divisive labels (nationality, party, etc.) should be criticized for producing prejudice and conflict; by contrast, invoking 'man' promotes compassion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recourse to breaches of justice ('reason of state')
rubrics_metrics.description: All writers on the science of policy are agreed, and they agree with experience, that, all governments must frequently infringe the rules of justice to support themselves; that truth must give way to dissimulation; honesty to convenience; and humanity itself to the reigning interest. The whole of this mystery of iniquity is called the reason of state.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use as an evaluative criterion whether a government routinely justifies violating justice or moral truth under 'reason of state.' Systems that institutionalize such breaches should be judged harshly; the author treats this as a central paradox to reject.

rubrics_metrics.name: Presence and use of coercive instruments and cruel punishments
rubrics_metrics.description: Let us take a review of the dungeons, whips, chains, racks, gibbets, with which every society is abundantly stored; by which hundreds of victims are annually offered up to support a dozen or two in pride and madness, and millions in an abject servitude and dependence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The existence and routine use of physical coercion, torture, and degrading punishments is a concrete metric of an institution's injustice and moral failure. Catalogues of instruments of punishment are cited as evidence of institutional corruption.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proximity to innate moral axioms (natural liberty/religion) as standard
rubrics_metrics.description: We have implanted in us by Providence, ideas, axioms, rules, of what is pious, just, fair, honest, which no political craft, nor learned sophistry can entirely expel from our breasts. By these we judge, and we cannot otherwise judge, of the several artificial modes of religion and society, and determine of them as they approach to or recede from this standard.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use innate moral intuitions—piety, justice, fairness, honesty—as the measuring stick for institutions. The author prescribes these natural axioms as the ultimate normative standard: evaluate each institution by how far it approaches or recedes from them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Indicators of despotism: arbitrary, capricious, and absolute rule
rubrics_metrics.description: The simplest form of government is despotism... The manner of ruling being directed merely by the will of the weakest, and generally the worst man in the society, becomes the most foolish and capricious thing, at the same time that it is the most terrible and destructive... The slightest displeasure is death.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify despotism by arbitrary exercise of power, capricious punishments, and the sovereign's detachment from accountability. These features are to be counted as decisive negative marks when assessing a government's legitimacy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Corruption via favorites and doubled tyranny
rubrics_metrics.description: There are two courts, and two interests; both very different from the interests of the people. The favorite knows that the regard of a tyrant is as unconstant and capricious as that of a woman; and concluding his time to be short, he makes haste to fill up the measure of his iniquity, in rapine, in luxury, and in revenge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether power is mediated through corrupt favorites who pursue private gain and accelerate oppression. The presence of competing courts or parallel centers of power multiplies tyranny and degrades governance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dehumanization and loss of dignity among the populace
rubrics_metrics.description: For the gross of the people, they are considered as a mere herd of cattle; and really in a little time become no better; all principle of honest pride, all sense of the dignity of their nature, is lost in their slavery.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measure the extent to which a political system strips citizens of dignity, pride, and moral worth. A polity that treats people as cattle and erodes civic virtue fails basic humanistic standards and should be judged and reformed accordingly.
